lessons.title: Arithmetic (+, -, *, /, %) & Assignment Operators (+=, -=)
lessons.description: Master the everyday math operators and the shorthand assignment shortcuts that make your code shorter and easier to read.

sections.heading: Arithmetic operators
paragraphs: JavaScript provides six basic math operators. They work on numbers and follow the standard rules of arithmetic you already know from math class.

sections.heading: Why remainder (%) is useful
paragraphs: The remainder operator gives you what is left over after dividing. It is surprisingly useful: check if a number is even (n % 2 === 0), cycle through array indices, or build repeating patterns.

sections.heading: Assignment operators
paragraphs: Assignment operators combine a math operation with storing the result. Instead of writing x = x + 5, you can write x += 5. They do the exact same thing but save you from repeating the variable name.

codeExamples.heading: Arithmetic in action
codeExamples.code:
let a = 10;
let b = 3;

console.log(a + b);   // 13
console.log(a - b);   // 7
console.log(a * b);   // 30
console.log(a / b);   // 3.3333...
console.log(a % b);   // 1
console.log(a ** b);  // 1000
explanation: The % (remainder) operator returns 1 because 10 divided by 3 is 3 with a remainder of 1.
** is the exponentiation operator — 10 ** 3 means 10 to the power of 3, which is 1000.
Division always returns a decimal result, even when both numbers are integers (e.g. 6 / 2 gives 3, not 3.0).

codeExamples.heading: Assignment operators in practice
explanation: Each assignment operator reads the current value, performs the math, and stores the result back in the same variable.
Notice that score %= 10 gives 5 — the remainder of 65 divided by 10.
These shortcuts are used everywhere in real code, especially for counters, accumulators, and score tracking.

practice.task: Create a variable total set to 0. Use += to add 25, then -= to subtract 10, then *= to double it, then %= to find the remainder when divided by 7. Print the result after each step.
hints: Start with let total = 0;
After total += 25;, total should be 25.
After total -= 10;, total should be 15.
After total *= 2;, total should be 30.
After total %= 7;, total should be 2.
practice.note: Assignment operators always update the variable in place — no need to write total = total + 25.

keyTakeaways: JavaScript has six arithmetic operators: +, -, *, /, %, and **.
The remainder operator (%) is great for checking even/odd numbers and cycling through patterns.
Assignment shortcuts (+=, -=, *=, etc.) combine math and assignment into one clean step.
Assignment operators work the same way for all numeric operations — they always store the result back in the same variable.
lessons.challenge: Write a tip calculator: start with a bill variable set to 85. Add a 15% tip using bill += bill * 0.15. Then round down to the nearest dollar using Math.floor(). Print the final amount.

lessons.title: Comparison Operators (<, >, <=, >=) & Strict Equality (=== vs ==)
lessons.description: Learn how JavaScript compares values — and why you should almost always use the strict versions.

sections.heading: Relational comparison operators
paragraphs: These operators compare two values and return true or false. They work as you would expect for numbers, and in a useful way for strings (alphabetical order).

sections.heading: Strict equality (=== and !==)
paragraphs: The triple-equal operator === checks if two values are exactly the same — same value AND same type. "5" === 5 is false because one is a string and the other is a number. This is the operator you should use 99% of the time.

sections.heading: Loose equality (== and !=)
paragraphs: The double-equal operator == tries to convert values to the same type before comparing. "5" == 5 is true because JavaScript converts the string to a number. This can cause surprising bugs — prefer === instead.

sections.heading: Why strict equality is better
paragraphs: Loose equality can produce unexpected results: 0 == false is true, "" == false is true, and null == undefined is true. Strict equality avoids all of these surprises. Most linters and style guides recommend always using === and !==.

codeExamples.heading: Comparison operators with numbers
codeExamples.code:
console.log(5 > 3);     // true
console.log(5 < 3);     // false
console.log(5 >= 5);    // true
console.log(5 <= 4);    // false

console.log(10 > 10);   // false
console.log(10 >= 10);  // true
explanation: These work exactly like you would expect from math. >= means "greater than OR equal to".
Use >= or <= when you want to include the boundary value.

codeExamples.heading: === vs == in practice
codeExamples.code:
// Strict equality (recommended)
console.log(5 === 5);           // true
console.log("5" === 5);         // false (different types)
console.log(null === undefined); // false

// Loose equality (avoid)
console.log(5 == 5);            // true
console.log("5" == 5);          // true  (string converted to number!)
console.log(null == undefined); // true  (surprising!)
explanation: === checks both value AND type — "5" === 5 is false because string ≠ number.
== performs type coercion before comparing — "5" == 5 converts the string to a number first, giving true.
Always prefer === to avoid bugs from unexpected type conversions.

practice.task: Write a function isAdult(age) that returns true if age is 18 or above, false otherwise. Test with 17, 18, 21, and "18" (string). Note which test case might be tricky.
hints: Use age >= 18 as your comparison.
If you pass "18" as a string, "18" >= 18 actually works because of type coercion.
To be safe, check typeof age === "number" first.
practice.note: Think about why "18" >= 18 is true but "18" === 18 is false.

keyTakeaways: Use <, >, <=, >= to compare values — they work on numbers and strings.
=== (strict equality) checks value AND type — use this almost always.
== (loose equality) converts types before comparing — it can produce surprising results.
When in doubt, use === and !==. Most style guides require them.
lessons.challenge: Write a function that takes two values and returns one of three strings: "equal" if both ===, "loosely equal" if == but not ===, or "not equal" otherwise. Test it with the pairs: (5, 5), ("5", 5), ("5", "5"), (0, false), and (null, undefined).

lessons.title: Logical Operators (&&, ||, !) & Short-Circuit Evaluation
lessons.description: Use AND, OR, and NOT to combine conditions — and discover how JavaScript "short-circuits" to skip unnecessary work.

sections.heading: The three logical operators
paragraphs: Logical operators combine or invert boolean values. They are the building blocks of conditional logic in every program.
list: && (AND) — returns true only if both sides are true
|| (OR) — returns true if at least one side is true
! (NOT) — flips true to false and vice versa

sections.heading: Short-circuit evaluation
paragraphs: JavaScript does not always evaluate both sides of a logical operator. It stops as soon as the result is determined — this is called short-circuiting.
list: && short-circuits on the first falsy value: if the left side is false, the right side is never evaluated
|| short-circuits on the first truthy value: if the left side is true, the right side is never evaluated

sections.heading: Truthiness: what counts as true or false?
paragraphs: JavaScript treats some values as falsy (treated as false) and everything else as truthy (treated as true). Falsy values: false, 0, "" (empty string), null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy — including "0", [], and {}.

codeExamples.heading: Logical operators with booleans
explanation: && (AND) returns true only when both sides are true.
|| (OR) returns true if either side is true.
! (NOT) flips the value — true becomes false and vice versa.

codeExamples.heading: Short-circuit evaluation in practice
codeExamples.code:
// && returns the first falsy value, or the last value if all truthy
console.log("hello" && 42);        // 42 (both truthy, returns last)
console.log(false && "hello");     // false (short-circuits here)
console.log(null && "hello");      // null

// || returns the first truthy value, or the last value if all falsy
console.log("hello" || 42);        // "hello" (short-circuits here)
console.log(false || "hello");     // "hello"
console.log(0 || null || "yes");   // "yes" (skips 0 and null)
explanation: Logical operators do not always return true/false — they return one of the actual values.
&& returns the first falsy value it finds, or the last value if all are truthy.
|| returns the first truthy value it finds, or the last value if all are falsy.

practice.task: Create variables username and age. Use && to check if both are truthy. Use || to provide a default value: let displayName = username || "Anonymous";. Test with empty strings and numbers.
hints: Try let username = ""; — an empty string is falsy, so || will use the default.
Try let age = 0; — zero is falsy, so age || 18 gives 18.
Use console.log(username && age); to see what && returns.
practice.note: Understanding that && and || return actual values (not just true/false) is a key insight.

keyTakeaways: && (AND) returns true only when both sides are truthy; || (OR) returns true when at least one side is truthy.
Short-circuiting means JavaScript stops evaluating as soon as the result is determined.
Logical operators return actual values, not just booleans — && returns the first falsy or last value; || returns the first truthy or last value.
Falsy values include: false, 0, "", null, undefined, NaN.
lessons.challenge: Write a function greet(name) that returns "Hello, World!" if no name is provided, or "Hello, [name]!" if a name is given. Use || for the default. Then write a second version using the && operator to build a greeting only when the name is truthy.

lessons.title: Modern Expression Operators: Nullish Coalescing (??) & Optional Chaining (?.)
lessons.description: Use the two most useful modern operators — nullish coalescing for safe defaults and optional chaining for safe property access.

sections.heading: Nullish coalescing (??)
paragraphs: The ?? operator is like || but smarter about defaults. It only falls back to the right side when the left side is null or undefined — it does NOT treat 0, "", or false as empty. This makes it perfect for default values where 0 or "" are valid.

sections.heading: Optional chaining (?.)
paragraphs: Optional chaining safely accesses nested properties without throwing an error. If any part of the chain is null or undefined, the whole expression returns undefined instead of crashing. You can use it with properties (obj?.prop), array access (arr?.[0]), and function calls (func?.()).

sections.heading: When to use ?? vs ||
paragraphs: Use ?? when 0, "", or false are valid values you want to keep. Use || when you want any falsy value to trigger the default. For example: score ?? 100 keeps a score of 0, but score || 100 would replace it with 100.

codeExamples.heading: Nullish coalescing vs OR
explanation: || replaced 0 and "" with defaults because they are falsy.
?? only replaced null with the default — 0 and "" were kept because they are not null/undefined.
This is the key difference: ?? is more precise about what counts as "missing".

codeExamples.heading: Optional chaining for safe access
explanation: user.address?.city checks if address exists before trying to access city.
If address is null or undefined, the expression returns undefined instead of throwing a TypeError.
Optional chaining works at any depth: stranger.address?.zip?.code safely checks each level.

practice.task: Create a user object with name and settings (which has theme). Use optional chaining to safely access user.settings?.theme. Then test with a user that has no settings property. Use ?? to provide a default theme of "light".
hints: Try user.settings?.theme ?? "light" — this combines both operators.
If settings is missing, ?. returns undefined, and ?? supplies "light".
Test with let user2 = { name: "Sam" }; — no settings at all.
practice.note: Optional chaining is one of the most practical features in modern JavaScript — you will use it constantly when working with API responses.

keyTakeaways: ?? (nullish coalescing) returns the right side only when the left is null or undefined — it keeps 0, "", and false.
?. (optional chaining) safely accesses nested properties — returns undefined instead of crashing.
Use ?? over || when 0 or "" are valid values you want to preserve.
Optional chaining works with properties, array indices, and method calls.
lessons.challenge: Build a settings object: { theme: "dark", fontSize: 0 }. Use ?? to load defaults — default theme should be "light", default font size should be 16. Notice that fontSize ?? 16 keeps 0 while fontSize || 16 would replace it. Then add optional chaining to safely access a nested user.profile?.avatar property that doesn't exist.

lessons.title: Logical Assignment Operators (&&=, ||=, ??=)
lessons.description: Combine logical operators with assignment to write shorter, more expressive code — the modern way to set defaults and conditional values.

sections.heading: What are logical assignment operators?
paragraphs: Logical assignment operators combine a logical check with an assignment in one step. They were introduced in ES2021 and are now supported in all modern browsers. There are three: &&=, ||=, and ??=.

sections.heading: The three operators
list: x &&= y is shorthand for x && (x = y) — assigns only if x is truthy
x ||= y is shorthand for x || (x = y) — assigns only if x is falsy
x ??= y is shorthand for x ?? (x = y) — assigns only if x is null/undefined

sections.heading: When to use each one
list: ||= is great for setting defaults when a variable is falsy (empty string, 0, null, undefined)
??= is better for defaults when 0 or "" are valid values you want to keep
&&= is less common — use it when you only want to update a variable if it already has a truthy value

codeExamples.heading: Logical assignment in action
explanation: ||= replaced the empty string with "dark" because "" is falsy.
||= also replaced 0 with 10 — this is a common gotcha. If 0 is a valid value, use ??= instead.
??= kept 0 because it only triggers on null/undefined.
??= supplied "blue" because color was undefined.

codeExamples.heading: &&= for conditional updates
explanation: &&= only assigns the new value if the current value is truthy.
This is useful when you want to transform a value but only if it exists — it acts as a guard.
If the variable is null, undefined, 0, "", or false, no assignment happens.

practice.task: Create a config object with a theme property set to "" and a fontSize property set to 0. Use ??= to set defaults: theme should default to "light", fontSize should stay 0 because it's not null/undefined.
hints: Use config.theme ??= "light"; — this will set theme to "light" because it's an empty string.
Wait — actually ??= only triggers on null/undefined, not empty strings. So "" ??= "light" keeps the empty string.
For the theme, you might want ||= instead: config.theme ||= "light";.
practice.note: This exercise shows the real-world decision between ||= and ??= — choose based on whether empty strings are valid values.

keyTakeaways: ||= assigns a new value only when the variable is falsy — great for defaults, but replaces 0 and "" too.
??= assigns only when the variable is null or undefined — safer when 0 or "" are valid.
&&= assigns only when the variable is truthy — useful for conditional transformations.
These operators make code shorter and more readable than writing out the full logical-then-assign pattern.
lessons.challenge: Write a function that takes a config object and fills in missing values using ??=. The defaults should be: theme: "light", fontSize: 16, language: "en". Pass in { theme: "dark" } and verify that only the missing properties get defaults.

lessons.title: Explicit Type Conversion (Number(), String(), Boolean())
lessons.description: Convert values between types on purpose — and understand why letting JavaScript do it automatically often leads to bugs.

sections.heading: Why convert types explicitly?
paragraphs: JavaScript often converts types automatically (called type coercion), but the rules are inconsistent and surprising. For example, "5" - 3 works (gives 2) but "5" + 3 gives "53". Explicit conversion using Number(), String(), and Boolean() makes your intent clear and avoids these surprises.

sections.heading: Boolean() — converting to booleans
paragraphs: Remember the falsy values from 1.5.3? Boolean() converts anything to a boolean using those same rules. Every falsy value becomes false; everything else becomes true.

codeExamples.heading: Converting user input to numbers
explanation: User input from forms, prompts, and URLs is always a string. You must convert it before doing math.
Number() successfully converts valid numeric strings. Invalid strings produce NaN.
Always validate with isNaN() after conversion to catch bad input.

codeExamples.heading: String and Boolean conversions
explanation: String() is the clearest way to convert any value to a string.
Boolean() follows the same falsy rules from 1.5.3 — empty strings and zero become false.
Empty arrays [] are truthy, so Boolean([]) is true. This surprises many beginners.

practice.task: Write a function safeAdd(a, b) that converts both inputs to numbers using Number(), then returns their sum. Test with "10" and "20", "5.5" and 3, and "abc" and 4. Handle the NaN case.
hints: Use Number(a) and Number(b) to convert.
Check isNaN() on the results to detect bad input.
Return a descriptive message like "Invalid input" if either is NaN.
practice.note: Try using parseInt() and parseFloat() as alternatives — they parse strings differently than Number().

keyTakeaways: Number() converts strings to numbers; invalid strings produce NaN. Always validate after converting.
String() converts any value to a string — it is the clearest and most reliable way.
Boolean() converts using falsy rules: 0, "", null, undefined, and NaN become false.
Prefer explicit conversion over relying on JavaScript's automatic type coercion — it prevents surprising bugs.
lessons.challenge: Write a function convertAndCompare(a, b) that: (1) converts both inputs to numbers, (2) returns "equal" if they are the same number, "a is bigger" if a > b, or "b is bigger" if b > a, and (4) returns "invalid input" if either conversion fails. Test it with ("10", "20"), ("5", "5"), ("abc", "5"), and ("3.14", "3").
